title: Does a measured walking-side preference pin down how many robots tip a crowd's passing side?
lede: Fitting the stubborn-bloc model to the side preference Moussaïd et al. (2009) measured for two head-on walkers (about 17.5% left, read from their Fig. 4) puts the mean-field tipping robot share at 0.075 to 0.096 for memory 9 across error rates 0.02 to 0.30, against 0.217 for an unbiased crowd; memory matters more (0.033 to 0.053 at 5, 0.133 to 0.149 at 17) and a stubborn-right bloc raises it.
summary: society-blocs swept the share of always-left people by hand. Here the share is fitted instead: the status-quo crowd must show the left share Moussaïd et al. (2009, Proc. R. Soc. B 276) measured when two walkers meet head on, which I read from their Fig. 4 bars as 0.175 (static obstacle: 0.40; the paper prints no numbers, reading error about 0.01). Always-left share and error rate trade off along the fit (at memory 9: 0.155 at ε = 0.02 down to 0.019 at 0.30), yet the tipping robot share barely moves along it: 0.075 to 0.096, against 0.217 with no bias. Memory length and a stubborn-right bloc move it more (memory 5: 0.033–0.053; 17: 0.133–0.149; with 30% always-right, 0.135–0.151 at memory 9). Simulation (200 people, 12 seeds) reproduces the left share (0.170–0.171) and tips 0 of 12 crowds 0.04 below and 12 of 12 0.04 above the mean-field value. Limits: one binary game in a well-mixed crowd, two walkers in a corridor are not a crowd, the bar heights are read from a figure, and the measured pairs may be partly stubborn and partly noisy in ways this cannot tell apart.
